newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: FOCUS - Venezuela holds all the cards in oil round.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Venezuela holds all the cards in oil round.

text.p: A prime cut of Venezuela's oil country is due to go under the hammer next week in a bidding round likely to attract strong bids from international companies, analysts said on Friday.

Limited risk and quick returns on investment are two key factors luring the world's oil barons to Caracas. The success of previous rounds has helped calm any possible worries about Venezuela's "apertura", or opening to private capital.
Some 131 companies, of which 45 Venezuelan, are expected to bid for operating licenses in 20 fields.
The process lasts five days, allowing companies time to modify their bids on later fields depending on early results.

It may seem odd that companies should be lining up to pay millions for the privilege of a contract where the government takes 91 percent of revenues after established costs, forcing operators to boost efficiency to get decent returns.
But with 73 billion barrels of proven oil reserves, the largest in the western hemisphere, analysts say Venezuela is holding all the cards.

"If I took a poll of my client base, certainly Venezuela is by far the most interesting opportunity on the oil side," said Sondra Scott, Latin America energy analyst for Cambridge Energy Research Associates.

Although the terms are tough, most operators have seen good returns on the licenses awarded in 1991 and 1993. The contract can also provide a strategic base from which to take advantage of other opportunities.

"In Venezuela you know you can grow your business because of the large geological base and this doesn't exist anywhere else in the region," said Rafael Quijano, Latin American energy analyst for Petroleum Finance Corp.

Other opportunities for foreign investors include profit- sharing exploration, outsourcing contracts and joint-ventures in the Orinoco bitumen fields, petrochemicals, coal and speciality refined products.

Quijano said the 20 blocks present a broad range of exploration and engineering risk. They include onshore, offshore and lake locations, light and heavy reserves, and a big range of previous exploration and production activity.

The 20 fields are split equally between the eastern and western ends of the country. In general they are larger than those offered in previous operating rounds. Companies will be allowed to undertake more exploration, both in deeper strata of existing discoveries and in adjacent areas.

Five blocks are reserved for Venezuelan operators and these have relatively low likelihood of major new finds, but also have lower investment requirements. Venezuelan operators need only take a 30-percent stake in these fields and some are expected to team up with foreign companies in consortia.
Unlike previous rounds, fields in this round will be awarded under a system whereby all participants pledge the same, fixed minimum investment and then bid on top of that to get the contract.
This system was introduced in the 1995 profit-sharing exploration round, when companies paid cash bids of $240 million for 10 contracts.
Contracting outside operators is part of PDVSA's 10-year $60 billion strategy to double oil production.

PDVSA wants to boost production to 6.2 million barrels per day (bpd) in 2006 from 3.4 million in 1996. It expects most of the new output to come from fields operated by private companies, which should generate investment dollars and bring state-of-the-art technology and management skills that have been lost in the 20 years since nationalisation.

Petroleos de Venezuela exploration chief Juan Szabo said he expected $5 billion of investment in the third round fields over the next 10 years, lifting output from 67,000 bpd currently to 350,000 bpd.
Venezuela's oil market liberalisation could not have come at a better time, analysts say.
It coincides with a period of rising world oil prices when companies have more cash to spend on oil production projects, and Venezuela's terms and timing beat its neighbours, Colombia and Brazil.
"Competition is regional ... But Colombia has failed to adjust its terms to meet the competitive challenge, and in Brazil the opening has not taken place yet," Quijano said.

Production from fields operated under the first two rounds recently exceeded 200,000 bpd and is expected to reach 400,000 in ten years. By then, PDVSA expects fields with private participation to account for a third of its 6 million bpd production.
((--Caracas newsroom, 582 505 2611))
